Six resellers who source bags directly from Hermes shoppers said access to a Birkin is generally linked to spending on Hermes scarves, clothes and shoes, although the exact policy differs between regions and stores. Two estimated customers typically spend $10,000 to $20,000 before being offered the Birkin or the Kelly, the brand's other popular bag. Hermes, which says a Birkin takes 15 hours to craft, does not disclose its selling policies or how many bags it makes. It declined to comment for this story. Of the nine Birkin resellers Reuters interviewed in the US, Europe and Asia, six said resale prices had fallen over the past year as more handbags became available, while five reported softer demand. Antoinette Hunter, who founded luxury handbag reseller Lilac Blue in 2007, said when she got the first request for a Birkin, few people knew the bag. She eventually sourced one from a member of Japan’s royal family. Acquiring Birkins is no longer a challenge, Hunter said, but it's harder to make money from resales. She said the price for an unworn black Birkin 25 bag, one of the most sought-after models, has fallen by around £4,000 ($5,336) since 2022, to around £24,000. Cai, who sells via Vestiaire Collective and Instagram, says his price for the bag is around £20,000. Hermes sells the same model for £9,390 in Britain, a Hermes sales assistant in London said. Although Hunter still sees plenty of demand for Hermès bags, particularly the most high-end ones, she said the decline in resale prices might dissuade some from buying directly from Hermes. "If Hermes continues to raise the prices, and the prices on the resale market continue to drop, that margin gets squeezed, and perhaps it will become less appealing," she said. Brokerage Bernstein, which tracks individual auction results, said in a September note the resale price on Birkin 25 bags averaged about 1.7 times the retail tag in the third quarter, down from about 2.6 times at their 2022 peak. BUSINESS MODEL UNDER SCRUTINY Hermes' leather goods division, which includes other handbag models, generates 44% of annual group revenue. For more than a decade, limited supply and strong demand allowed Birkins to command hefty resale premiums, benefiting both Hermes and resellers as the prospects of making a profit via the secondary market encouraged Hermes clients to buy more from the brand. "It was a win-win," said Sarah Davis, founder of California-based Fashionphile. The company said its Birkin listings have grown 32-fold in 15 years. The company's website currently lists 212 Birkins on sale. Hermes has gradually expanded the production of its handcrafted items, opening one workshop per year on average. Meanwhile, the rise of resale platforms such as Vestiaire Collective and The RealReal, alongside vintage boutiques with online shops and social media channels, has made it easier than ever to resell. The bags and other Hermes items remain highly sought after, resellers said, but the brand is showing some strain. Hermes’ shares have lost nearly 40% of their market value this year, making the brand one of the worst performers among listed luxury companies. Earlier this month, UBS analysts downgraded Hermes shares to "sell", saying that growing secondary-market supply of Birkins and Kellys could weaken the brand's scarcity-driven business model. "We believe the nature of the business is changing," they said in a note, estimating that the number of the handbags listed for sale worldwide is now six to seven times higher than before the pandemic. The company is expected to report quarterly sales growth of 5.2% on Thursday, which would mark its weakest quarterly growth in six years, according to Visible Alpha estimates. While leather goods revenue is still expected to grow by 10%, demand for clothing, silk scarves and perfumes is cooling, a sign fewer customers are making the purchases traditionally required to buy a Birkin at a later stage, two equities analysts and two industry consultants said. Asked in July whether Hermes should slow production to protect the brand, Hermes CEO Axel Dumas told reporters that some people feared making too many bags would hurt its exclusivity, while others questioned why it was not making more. He added that output depended largely on the number of fully trained artisans and available high-quality leather. Not all resellers see weakness. Davis said prices for the bag on the Fashionphile platform have remained firm and even risen slightly this year, pointing to renewed attention generated by Norwegian soccer star Erling Haaland's handbag collection. ($1 = 0.8911 euros)

item.title: US invokes rarely used torture law in revamped case against Maduro
item.description: Nicolas Maduro is one of just a handful of people to be charged in the US with violating a federal law criminalizing torture committed overseas, a Reuters review of court records found, as prosecutors seek to broaden their criminal case against the ousted Venezuelan president.
item.dc:creator: Luc Cohen
item.content:encoded: Nicolas Maduro is one of just a handful of people to be charged in the US with violating a federal law criminalizing [USN:L6N45U13M TEXT:"torture"] committed overseas, a Reuters review of court records found, as prosecutors seek to broaden their criminal case against the ousted Venezuelan president. Maduro, 63, and his wife Cilia Flores, 70, [USN:L6N461121 TEXT:"pleaded not guilty"] last week to an expanded indictment accusing them of conspiring to torture political opponents to remain in power, in addition to the drug trafficking charges they already faced. They are scheduled to go on trial in June 2027. Maduro and Flores, captured in January during a US military raid in Caracas ordered by President Donald Trump , are just the seventh and eighth people Reuters identified who have been charged with violating a 1994 law criminalizing acts of torture. The law defines torture as an act intended to inflict severe physical or mental pain or suffering on a person in custody. Four people have been convicted under the statute, including members of paramilitary forces in [USN:JOE50902R TEXT:"Liberia"] and [USN:L4N3UE1C5 TEXT:"Gambia"], the head of a [USN:L1N45912B TEXT:"Syrian prison"] under ousted President Bashar al-Assad, and a US citizen who developed an [USN:L4N2UT3P3 TEXT:"illegal arms factory"] in Iraq. The Maduro case marks the first time the United States has prosecuted a head of state for allegedly authorizing the use of torture in their country, according to Michel Paradis, a partner at the Steptoe law firm. "This really is a landmark case," said Paradis, who previously represented detainees at the Guantanamo Bay US naval base. The torture charges mark a substantial shift in the focus of the case against Maduro and Flores. While they remain accused of abusing their power to [USN:L6N3ZT19O TEXT:"help drug traffickers"] and enrich themselves, the new charges mean that alleged human rights abuses during the political upheaval that often marked Maduro's 13 years in office will become central to the trial. 'A SIGNIFICANT ESCALATION' The torture charge could strengthen the hand of prosecutors by allowing them to tell a more comprehensive story about how Maduro allegedly employed a wide range of criminal activity to stay in power, and by enabling them to call more sympathetic witnesses, legal experts said. "The torture charge is really a significant escalation," said Artie McConnell, a former federal prosecutor focused on national security issues. "It puts these torture and political repression elements at the center of the government's theory," McConnell added, referring to the prosecution. Lawyers for Maduro did not respond to requests for comment. Mark Donnelly and Andres Sanchez, lawyers for Flores, said she is "completely innocent" of all charges. They said they would revise a motion they previously made to dismiss the indictment on the basis of [USN:L6N44U15Y TEXT:"sovereign immunity"] — protection from prosecution as the head of a sovereign country — to account for the new charges. A spokesperson for the Manhattan US Attorney's office, which brought the charges, declined to comment. COOPERATING WITNESSES The 1994 law was passed by Congress to make good on US obligations under the United Nations Convention against Torture, signed during President Ronald Reagan's tenure. Under the law, each torture count is punishable by up to 20 years in prison, or by a life sentence or the death penalty if the victim dies due to the torture. People convicted of multiple acts of torture can receive longer sentences. Those convicted under the statute so far have received prison sentences of 60 to 97 years. Maduro and Flores are not eligible for the death penalty because they are charged with torture conspiracy, not with carrying out torture themselves. US prosecutors can bring torture charges only against defendants who are US nationals or who are physically present in the United States. The charges against Maduro and Flores came after they were brought to New York following the raid in Caracas. Many of the other defendants in US torture cases had moved to or attempted to enter the United States after the alleged torture. McConnell, a partner at law firm BakerHostetler, said the new indictment was more detailed than the previous one, citing the descriptions of alleged torture victims and incidents. In one 2018 incident described in the indictment, prosecutors said Venezuelan military officers hit a detainee with a machete and sprayed him with a chemical irritant while interrogating him about the whereabouts of a Maduro political opponent. Jurors could find testimony from alleged torture victims to be powerful, said Shane Stansbury, a former federal prosecutor in Manhattan. Three of the alleged torture victims in the indictment are American citizens, and their testimony could resonate particularly strongly among the jurors, McConnell said. A trial on the drug trafficking charges alone likely would have relied heavily on the testimony of cooperating witnesses, who may have played a role in the alleged crimes themselves. Defense lawyers often question cooperating witnesses sharply about their own criminal histories on cross-examination to try to undercut their credibility. To be sure, cooperating witnesses are still likely to prove critical in helping prosecutors link Maduro and Flores to the alleged torture, experts said. Kevin Sullivan, a prosecutor with the Manhattan US Attorney's office, said in an October 8 court hearing that cooperating witnesses would testify about alleged involvement by Maduro and Flores in the torture conspiracy. ACQUITTAL IN TENNESSEE Not every torture case the US has brought has resulted in a conviction. One defendant, an upstate New York resident named Sulejman Mujagic who was charged in the US in 2012 with torturing a soldier after the breakup of the former Yugoslavia, was instead extradited to Bosnia for trial in 2013. Another defendant charged over alleged torture in Bosnia, Sead Miljkovic, was found not guilty of US torture charges by a jury in Chattanooga, Tennessee, in 2025 but later pleaded guilty to passport fraud. He has since left the US, according to his lawyer, Bryan Hoss. Hoss said the accounts given by the alleged victims who testified in the case had shifted over time, undercutting their credibility, and that the abuse allegedly committed by his client did not rise to the level of torture. Hoss also said that jurors may have questioned why the US government was prosecuting the case. Jurors in the Maduro trial may not have similar concerns. "The fact that these are filed against the former head of the country allows people to understand it a little better," Hoss said.

item.title: Shark nicknamed 'Bukangi' returns to sea off South Korea after third rescue attempt
item.description: A shark that became a sensation after spending more than a month in a canal in the South Korean port of Busan was successfully guided back into the open sea on Wednesday, following two failed rescue attempts, the oceans ministry said.
item.dc:creator: Hyun Yi, Daewoung Kim
item.content:encoded: A shark that became a sensation after spending more than a month in a canal in the South Korean port of Busan was successfully guided back into the open sea on Wednesday, following two failed rescue attempts, the oceans ministry said. The shark, nicknamed "Bukangi", was first spotted in a narrow waterway on September 18. More than 1.6 million people visited the waterfront park through October 20 to catch a glimpse of it, according to the Busan Infrastructure Corporation. Lee Min-jeung, a 39-year-old travel content creator from Seoul, said she had travelled to Busan four times to see Bukangi. "I'm relieved that it seems to have returned to the sea," Lee said. "Goodbye. Don't get sick." South Korea's National Institute of Fisheries Science identified Bukangi as a female dusky shark measuring about 3 meters (10 feet) in length. WARMING WATERS COULD BE BEHIND SIGHTINGS The species, which inhabits tropical, subtropical and temperate waters, is classified as endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature. Bukangi's appearance has also drawn attention to changes in the waters around South Korea, with experts citing warming seas as one possible factor behind a rise in large shark sightings. The fisheries institute recorded 46 sightings of large sharks along the country's east coast in the first half of this year, compared with 12 during the same period last year. The shark's stay was unusual because the narrow canal lies near high-rise buildings and a major high-speed rail station in central Busan. The operation to free it was deemed necessary because the shark had not been observed feeding, and falling temperatures could affect its health, city officials said. South Korean media also said Bukangi had sustained minor injuries to its fin and snout. Authorities tried to guide it out on September 29 and October 2 but both attempts were unsuccessful. On Wednesday, authorities used a net attached to floating platforms and divers to navigate the canal's underwater terrain and varying depths. Workers moved the net toward the sea while preventing the shark from swimming back into the canal.

item.title: Russia says it will send first diesel cargo to US on Thursday
item.description: Russia will dispatch its first tanker with diesel for the United States on Thursday, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said, according to the Vedomosti news outlet, after a deal with US President Donald Trump.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Russia will dispatch its first tanker with diesel for the United States on Thursday, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said, according to the Vedomosti news outlet, after a deal with US President Donald Trump. Russia lifted its self-imposed ban on diesel exports on October 9, introduced to tackle domestic shortages triggered by Ukrainian drone attacks on refineries, after [USN:L1N45V0MW TEXT:"reaching the deal"] with Trump to supply diesel to global markets. Novak said on Wednesday the vessel will carry 40,000 metric tons of the fuel, adding that the paperwork on the fuel supply is nearing its completion, according to media reports. He did not name the port from which the cargo will be delivered. "Additional shipments will follow, of course. There were agreements reached between the two leaders. We will meet the United States' needs, to the extent of our capabilities," RIA news agency quoted Novak as saying. Trump has said Russia would immediately export 300,000 metric tons, or 2.25 million barrels, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter". The US exports about 1.5 million barrels of diesel per day. Russian President Vladimir Putin [USN:L6N4670LA TEXT:"was hosting"] US special envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday, after the US-Russia diesel export deal led to a sharp deterioration in ties between the United States and Ukraine. During the talks in St Petersburg, Witkoff thanked Putin for lifting the export restrictions. Putin also mentioned the deal, saying that global diesel prices dropped by 5%-6% after the agreement. "That's an example of us working together, I want to thank you for that," Witkoff said in televised comments. Putin also said that first Russian tankers with diesel will departs in two to three days. "We are preparing deliveries of several vessels, the tankers, right now. They will go one after another. The financial component should be provided," he said, adding that Russia also would be able to supply fertilisers in "large quantities" to the US market.

item.title: Yemen's Houthis deny launching drones towards Saudi Arabia's Medina
item.description: Yemen's Houthis said that they had neither launched drones towards the Saudi holy city of Medina on Wednesday nor conducted military operations towards Saudi Arabia, refuting earlier comments from the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Yemen's Houthis said that they had neither launched drones towards the Saudi holy city of Medina on Wednesday nor conducted military operations towards Saudi Arabia, refuting earlier comments from the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen. The comments by the Iran-aligned group's military spokesperson Yahya Saree follow the coalition saying that it had intercepted drones over Medina and the Eastern region. The Houthis had warned airlines this month against using the Saudi airspace as they intensified attacks on the kingdom, the world's largest oil exporter, saying only the airspace over Islam's holy cities of Mecca and Medina would be exempted. The Houthis have attacked [USN:L1N45W03M TEXT:"Riyadh's international airport"] and state oil giant [USN:L1N45Z0HH TEXT:"Saudi Aramco"], disrupting flights and oil exports. Yemen, one of the world's worst humanitarian crises, has been mired in a civil war since 2014 when the Houthis drove the government out of the northern capital, drawing Saudi-led military intervention. Renewed fighting in recent weeks ended a 2022 UN-brokered truce that had largely halted cross-border attacks between a Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognised government and the Houthis, who controls the capital Sanaa. The escalation has opened another front in the US-Israeli war on Iran . Within Yemen, the Houthis claimed an attack on Wednesday on a military camp near the airport in the southern city of Aden, where the Yemeni government is based. A government military source and a local official told Reuters the group also attacked Riyan airport in the southeastern coastal city of Mukalla. A Houthi missile attack on a government security forces training camp in Yemen's Shabwa province on Monday [USN:L1N4660GJ TEXT:"killed 73 people"].

item.title: Trump envoy asks Putin to resume three-way Ukraine peace talks, secures release of US citizen
item.description: US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to review new ideas on ending the war amid Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War Two.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday urged Russian President Vladimir Putin to consider resuming US-mediated peace talks with Ukraine and to review new ideas on ending the war amid Washington's latest push to stop Europe's bloodiest conflict since World War Two. The talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia - the release of [USN:L8N4670PP TEXT:"Stephen Hubbard, a retired US school teacher"] held in Russia. Putin also offered to help US President Donald Trump in dealing with Iran, saying Russia had a decades-long relationship with Tehran which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran's nuclear programme. Russia could also supply large quantities of fertiliser to the United States to help US farmers, the Russian president told Witkoff, saying he wanted to discuss [USN:L1N4650BJ TEXT:"a potential meeting in China next month"] with Trump which the Kremlin has suggested could also include Chinese President Xi Jinping. The encounter comes amid concerns in Kyiv and among its allies that the United States is backing away from Ukraine, at times holding back real-time intelligence on Russian attacks and hobbling Ukraine's military communications. The latest talks also come more than two years since Trump promised in his successful election campaign to end the Ukraine war within 24 hours. "One thing that I hope to accomplish today is to have some good conversation between us about the resumption potentially of trilateral talks between Ukraine and Russia and the United States," Witkoff told Putin. "Even if we don't have a resolution today, if we just talk about and sort of consider what that next step might be I think that would be important and the world is waiting to hear that". The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran . Ukraine and Russia remain far apart when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal, but Trump has recently intensified pressure on Ukraine to strike some kind of a deal. He said on Tuesday it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face "a very bad thing." 'NEW IDEAS' Putin, who has shown few signs of compromising on his central war aims, which include full Russian control of the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine and no NATO membership for Kyiv, received Witkoff in the Constantine Palace, a grand imperial edifice in what is the Kremlin chief's home city. Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's special investment envoy, was also present at the meeting with Witkoff as both sides talked up the potential of post-war Russia-US economic cooperation. Witkoff flew into Russia's second city a day after conducting [USN:L1N466099 TEXT:"talks"] in Oslo with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, the leaders of Finland and Norway and European and NATO representatives. Witkoff said he would brief Putin on the Oslo talks which he described as productive and said had been characterised by "some degree of momentum." He said he had brought some documents with him containing various ideas for a potential peace deal for Putin to review, and that Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, also wanted to convey some ideas to Putin and would shortly join the meeting remotely by phone. A US official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, said Ukraine had brought [USN:L1N466099 TEXT:"new ideas and proposals"] to the Oslo talks, which had made "meaningful progress" toward a coordinated approach to engaging with Russia. The official said the talks covered "key elements of a comprehensive peace framework," including security guarantees for Ukraine, a post-war economic plan and a broader European security architecture. Zelenskiy said he hoped to discuss key issues on how to end the war during a trilateral meeting with Putin and Trump. The Kremlin has repeatedly said that any Putin-Zelenskiy meeting would need to be painstakingly prepared in advance by aides to make it worthwhile. FRAYING US-UKRAINE TIES US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month to help lower prices in the United States. High fuel costs since he launched strikes on Iran have hurt his Republicans ahead of November legislative elections. Since the diesel deal, Ukraine has complained of disruption to some intelligence sharing and to its use of the Starshield military satellite system, though Zelenskiy said that Tuesday's Oslo meeting had reached an agreement to resolve those issues. Citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that billionaire Elon Musk had last week ordered the slowdown of a military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite service that Ukraine relies on to track Russian ballistic missile strikes. Reuters could not immediately verify the report. Musk has said any such decision is taken by the US military or the president. Trump has said he was not responsible and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reiterated on Wednesday that Washington had not pulled back Kyiv's ability to access Starlink.

item.title: Antitrust watchdog launches probe into Spain's Exolum over potential abuse
item.description: Spain's competition authority CNMC has opened sanctioning proceedings against Spanish energy logistics company Exolum over three suspected abuses of a dominant position, it said on Wednesday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Spain's competition authority CNMC has opened sanctioning proceedings against Spanish energy logistics company Exolum over three suspected abuses of a dominant position, it said on Wednesday. The CNMC is investigating Exolum's alleged imposition of excessive fees and its refusal to grant access to its transport and storage facilities to a competing third-party operator at the northeastern port of Tarragona. The potential abuses might have led to consumers facing successive price hikes, the CNMC said, adding that the conduct would have allowed Exolum to maintain high profit margins and strengthen its dominant position in a coastal area of significant economic importance. "A third competitor might have seen its right of access to Spain's only pipeline network for the transport of liquid hydrocarbons restricted and, consequently, its ability to compete in downstream markets," it added. Exolum said it will cooperate fully with the CNMC throughout the proceedings and that it will exercise its right to defend itself. The company said in a statement that it considers its prices reasonable and transparent, and that its conduct complies with competition law and regulations. "In fact, price changes for Exolum's main services have been below the rate of inflation every year for the past 25 years and have remained unchanged throughout the recent energy crisis," Exolum said. The watchdog has up to 24 months to resolve the investigation.

item.title: North Korea to activate anti-South loudspeakers along border
item.description: North Korea will activate anti-South Korea propaganda loudspeakers along its entire border by the end of October, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea’s leader, said on Wednesday, escalating tensions on the heavily fortified frontier.
item.dc:creator: Joyce Lee, Kyu-Seok Shim
item.content:encoded: North Korea will activate anti-South Korea propaganda loudspeakers along its entire border by the end of October, Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea ’s leader, said on Wednesday, escalating tensions on the heavily fortified frontier. The move threatens to reverse one of South Korean President Lee Jae Myung's most-touted achievements in [USN:L1N43P0BF TEXT:"easing tensions"] with Pyongyang after his administration halted South Korea’s broadcasts and dismantled its fixed loudspeakers last year. In a scathing statement carried by state media KCNA after a visit to the border, Kim said North Korean tactical units were taking up new positions and called the border-wide loudspeaker deployment “the most legitimate measure and an appropriate response" to South Korea's measures. "Our tactical hunting teams are taking new positions, and within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border," she said, using the acronym for South Korea 's formal name, the Republic of Korea. KIM VISITED LOCATIONS ALONG THE BORDER She said she had visited several locations along the border early on Wednesday with North Korean Army Marshal Pak Jong Chon and found that the frontier was clearly blocked and becoming increasingly fortified. Kim accused South Korean forces of issuing loudspeaker warnings and firing warning shots in at least two locations on Wednesday. North Korean troops were exercising restraint and preparing thoroughly for any contingency, she said. "If the enemy’s provocative warning fire goes beyond its stated purpose and results in actual harm to the safety of our territory or our soldiers, our border troops will mercilessly eliminate the armed thugs who have lost their reason,” she said. The report came a day after Seoul pledged to punish "resolutely" any further provocation by Pyongyang if North Korea acted on threats to strengthen its military posture along the border. Kim said new firepower units had "taken their firing positions" at the border, KCNA reported. ARMY MARSHAL URGES 'IMPREGNABLE FORTRESS' AT BORDER Tensions between North and South Korea have risen since Pyongyang began fortifying its border in April 2024. The two countries are separated by the Demilitarized Zone that was established when the Korean War ended in an armistice in 1953. Seoul says Pyongyang has sent up to 7,000 workers to the border this year, with about 50 crossings of the Military Demarcation Line, which bisects the DMZ, to South Korea's side of the border. On Wednesday, North Korea rejected Seoul's allegations, with Pak dismissing the claim as an "absurd assertion" designed to shift blame, KCNA reported. The North Korean army knew where the border lay "better than any others" and was only doing what it should within its own territory, Pak said, urging soldiers to turn the border into an "impregnable fortress". South Korea said North Korean mines caused a [USN:L1N45S029 TEXT:"border blast"] last month that seriously wounded two of its soldiers, and called on Pyongyang to suspend the fortification work.

item.title: UK borrowing and £3 trillion debt herald tough budget for Healey
item.description: Britain's government borrowed more than expected again in September and public debt surpassed £3 trillion ($4.01 trillion), according to official data that underscored finance minister John Healey's challenge in his first budget next week.
item.dc:creator: William Schomberg
item.content:encoded: Britain's government borrowed more than expected again in September and public debt surpassed £3 trillion ($4.01 trillion), according to official data that underscored finance minister John Healey's challenge in his first budget next week. Economists said the figures added to the likelihood of Healey delivering a cautious set of spending, tax and borrowing plans on October 28. Borrowing hit £24.52 billion last month, up from £22.76 billion in the same month last year, as spending on debt interest rose. It was also higher than a median forecast of £23.85 billion in a Reuters poll of economists. Over the first six months of the 2026/27 fiscal year, the deficit stood at £97.8 billion, down by £4.4 billion from a year earlier but £6 billion above the forecast made by the Office for Budget Responsibility, which was made before the Iran war began. Healey is expected to [USN:L8N4610PT TEXT:"raise taxes on banks"] among other measures next week to stay on track to meet his fiscal rules. Separate data published by the Office for National Statistics on Wednesday showed [USN:L8N46708O TEXT:"inflation rose"] by more than expected in September, which is likely to add to calls for more support for poorer households in his budget. But analysts at Capital Economics said the higher-than-expected borrowing in recent months "reinforces our view that the chancellor will deliver a cautious budget on 28th October that has little net impact on the economy and leaves the toughest fiscal choices for next year." Healey's margin for error to stay on course to meet his main budget target is expected to have narrowed sharply in large part due to the rise in borrowing costs for government debt around the world since the start of the conflict in the Gulf. UK government debt interest costs - which are pushed up when inflation rises - jumped by almost 17% in September to almost £11 billion and were up by nearly 4% over the April-to-September period at £60.8 billion pounds. Overall government spending was up by 7% in September when tax receipts rose by 5.2%, the ONS said. But over the first six months of the tax year, spending grew by slightly less than tax income. Healey's main target is to balance day-to-day spending with tax revenue by the 2029/30 tax year. The ONS said the current budget was bigger in September than in the same month last year. Over the first six months of the tax year it stood at £64 billion, down by more than 8%. Public sector debt was estimated to have exceeded £3 trillion for the first time. However, as a proportion of the economy, debt was lower than a year earlier, the ONS said. ($1 = 0.7481 pounds)

item.title: OPmobility's revenue rises amid reorganization, weak auto market
item.description: OPmobility reported higher third-quarter revenue on Wednesday, even as the French car parts supplier restructures its business amid broader auto industry weakness.
item.dc:creator: Mathias Rozario, Etienne Breban
item.content:encoded: OPmobility (OPM.PA) reported higher third-quarter revenue on Wednesday, even as the French car parts supplier restructures its business amid broader auto industry weakness. The company's consolidated revenue rose 2.8% on a like-for-like basis to €2.44 billion ($2.74 billion), driven by growth across its business areas. Its exterior and lighting solutions unit, which makes up 44% of total revenue and holds leading market positions in bumpers and tailgates, continued to lead the performance. The global picture, however, remained uneven. OPmobility's like-for-like sales underperformed Mobility Global's automotive production forecast in North America and Asia, falling 5.9% and 11.6%, respectively. “China, in particular, remains pretty challenging,” CEO Félicie Burelle said in a post-earnings call. Domestic vehicle sales in China fell 24% in the quarter, making it a critical and tense market for the company, she added. Meanwhile, European sales growth of 8.6% outperformed the broader market. "It was mainly driven by our activity in Eastern Europe," Burelle said. "In Western Europe, however, we still do see a weaker demand, with some additional shutdowns that have been communicated over the last weeks." Earlier in October, OPmobility [USN:L6N45T12N TEXT:"lowered"] its 2026 targets and said it would cut about 770 jobs in Europe, citing lower automotive production forecasts, changes in customer activity and delays in the hydrogen mobility market. Burelle said raw material inflation, especially in resins and components like printed circuit boards and memory chips, has squeezed margins. Some pass-through mechanisms exist for these costs, but with a lag of three to six months, while negotiations with customers are becoming harder because automakers are also under pressure, she added. "The [USN:L6N4660XK TEXT:"decision to ease restrictions"] on combustion engine vehicles does not change much for OPmobility. We are sticking to a strategy of diversifying our propulsion systems," finance chief Olivier Dabi said during a press call. ($1 = 0.8903 euros)

item.title: Gold hits near one-week low on elevated oil prices
item.description: Gold prices held steady on Wednesday after touching their lowest level in nearly a week, as a rally in oil prices revived inflation concerns while investors awaited next week's Federal Reserve meeting for clues on the interest rate outlook.
item.dc:creator: Vishak Mathew
item.content:encoded: Gold prices held steady on Wednesday after touching their lowest level in nearly a week, as a rally in oil prices revived inflation concerns while investors awaited next week's Federal Reserve meeting for clues on the interest rate outlook. Spot gold was at $4,127.53 per ounce by 1045 GMT after hitting its lowest since October 15 in earlier trade. U.S. gold futures for December delivery rose 0.1% to $4,145.70 per ounce. "Gold has adhered to the downtrend that began 2 months ago on persistent expectations that more Fed rate hikes are in store," said Han Tan, chief market analyst at Bybit. While gold has long served as an inflation hedge, its lack of yield makes it less attractive when interest rates rise. Nearly all economists [USN:L6N46606V TEXT:"surveyed by Reuters"] expect the Federal Reserve to hold interest rates steady this month before delivering a hike in December, as policymakers opt for patience despite persistent inflation pressures that would otherwise call for stronger action. "Despite the expected pause at next week's FOMC meeting, Fed funds futures are fully pricing in one more 25-bps hike before the year comes to a close, with two more hikes expected by mid-2027," Tan added. Markets are also waiting for US Personal Consumption Expenditures data next week, the Fed's preferred gauge to monitor its 2% inflation target. Hotter-than-expected [USN:L1N45Z121 TEXT:"consumer"] and [USN:L1N4610KT TEXT:"producer"] inflation data last week showed that US price pressures remained elevated on soaring energy prices. Oil prices [USN:L1N46701N TEXT:"gained"] more than $1, with Brent futures holding above $110 a barrel, as escalating Middle East [USN:S8N44M08Y TEXT:"tensions"] fuelled fears of supply disruptions. Elsewhere, [USN:L8N46708O TEXT:"UK inflation"] hit an 11-month high of 3.5% in September, keeping the Bank of England on track to raise rates in November. Among other metals, spot silver slid 0.7% to $57.6 per ounce, platinum fell 0.4% to $1,642.25 and palladium dropped 1% to $1,091.87.

item.title: State Bank of India reports cyberattack involving nearly 3,900 customer records
item.description: State Bank of India on Wednesday reported a cyberattack involving 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information that was leaked on the dark web.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: State Bank of India (SBI.NS) on Wednesday reported a cyberattack involving 3,897 customer records containing personally identifiable information that was leaked on the dark web. The lender said a preliminary analysis showed that the exposed information included customer names, mobile numbers, dates of birth, email addresses, residential addresses, brand and customer identifiers, and loan records. SBI has engaged an independent cybersecurity agency to conduct a comprehensive assessment and investigate the nature and extent of the data leak. "Customer balances are completely safe," the lender said in a post on X. The leak is not expected to have any material impact on the bank's core business operations, financial performance or business continuity, SBI said. The incident comes amid heightened [USN:KCN0YO1FG TEXT:"regulatory focus"], with India's banking regulator pushing lenders to strengthen cybersecurity frameworks in recent years amid a rise in threats targeting financial institutions.

item.title: Earnings cheer supports stocks, France's 10-year bond yield hits 5% mark
item.description: Global stocks nudged up on Wednesday, as early signs from the earnings season pointed to strong profits for global firms and shored up sentiment in the face of nagging worries about the strength of the AI trade and turbulence in government bonds.
item.dc:creator: Dhara Ranasinghe, Gregor Hunter
item.content:encoded: Global stocks nudged up on Wednesday, as early signs from the earnings season pointed to strong profits for global firms and shored up sentiment in the face of nagging worries about the strength of the AI trade and turbulence in government bonds. Still, France's 10-year bond yield [USN:L8N4670MT TEXT:"hit 5%"] for the first time since 2002 in a sign of growing unease over its ability to restore its fragile finances, with violent protests adding to concern about the outlook for the euro zone's second-largest economy. World markets have had a rocky ride this month as a sharp [USN:L6N45Z12J TEXT:"selloff in AI-related shares"] has soured sentiment towards the tech sector. European markets were broadly higher (.STOXX) , while US stock futures , pointed to a positive open for Wall Street shares ahead of earnings reports from the likes of Meta (META.O) and Tesla (TSLA.O) later on. With 13% of S&P 500 companies reporting, 86% have beaten earnings estimates, according to LSEG data. "What we've seen over 2026 so far is effectively that markets have positively responded to strong earnings," said Neil Fisher, an investment specialist at St James's Place in London. "Where they have not always responded positively to stronger earnings, especially on the AI side of things, is when further CapEx (capital expenditure) and further spending on AI gets put on the table." In Asia, MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan (.MISX00000PUS) rallied around 1%, led by a more than 3% gain in Korea (.KS11) , while Japan's Nikkei 225 (.N225) rose almost 1%. AI WINNERS AND LOSERS Australian data centre operator NextDC (NXT.AX) shed nearly half of its market capitalisation on Wednesday after sharply cutting [USN:L4N4661TS TEXT:"revenue forecasts"] for the year ahead and putting future developments on hold, extending the burst of negative sentiment towards global AI stocks. In contrast, shares in South Korean artificial intelligence infrastructure company Elice Group (0158S0.KQ) [USN:P8N44T04P TEXT:"surged"] almost 30%, rebounding from a slump in its market debut on Tuesday. Shares in companies in Japan and Taiwan that are suppliers to Tesla (TSLA.O) and SpaceX (SPCX.O) advanced after Elon Musk said on Tuesday that a merger of the two companies would be "[USN:L4N4661M0 TEXT:"a good idea"]" and that they had formed special committees to discuss a union. Meanwhile in Mumbai, Jio Platforms' < JIOP.NS $3.2 billion IPO was [USN:L1N467028 TEXT:"fully subscribed"] in less than two hours of public bidding, as investors flocked to India's largest share sale and the first from billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance in two decades. WEAK SPOTS France's bond yields rose again as investors took stock of the [USN:L6N4660DJ TEXT:"widespread protests"] across the country that have piled pressure on a government already struggling to shore up its finances. Its 10-year bond yields have risen 20 basis points so far this week to hit a new 24-year high at 5.002%. That left the gap over 10-year German Bund yields at around 157 bps . "It's starting to look quite stressed," said Rushabh Amin, a portfolio manager for the multi-asset team at Allspring Global Investors. "The (French) OAT-Bund spread has been going in one direction for a while." French supermarket operator Carrefour (CARR.PA) fell almost 13% after cutting its [USN:L6N4670H2 TEXT:"guidance"] due to the recent protests. A rebound in the oil price [USN:L1N46701N TEXT:"back above $110 a"] barrel, after a short-lived drop the previous day, added to the negative sentiment across bond markets with US Treasury yields also rising in London trade . US envoy [USN:L6N4670LA TEXT:"Steve Witkoff met"] Russian President Vladimir Putin to review new ideas on ending the war in Ukraine, after what a US official called "constructive" talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Norway. INDONESIA LEAVES RATES ON HOLD Indonesia's central bank [USN:L4N466083 TEXT:"held"] its main interest rate unchanged on Wednesday, but raised its deposit facility rate by 25 basis points and cut banks' reserve requirement ratio by 2 percentage points to support liquidity and lending after markets were roiled by an MSCI warning last week that Indonesian stocks could be excluded from its major benchmarks. The rupiah slipped [USN:L4N4670LR TEXT:"back below the key 18,000 level"] to hold on to its title as the worst-performing Asian currency, down over 7% this year. The dollar index , which measures the currency against six peers, was a touch lower at 101.79, while the French jitters kept the euro on the defensive. The single currency was down around 0.12% at $1.122 . The yen was flat against the dollar at 158.15 after government data released on Wednesday showed [USN:L1N467001 TEXT:"Japan's exports"] in September rose 16.7% from a year earlier, missing estimates. Strong demand for semiconductors and AI-related products offset weakness in other sectors. Elsewhere, data showed UK inflation rose by 3.5%, while the government borrowed [USN:L8N46708T TEXT:"more than expected"] again in September and public debt surpassed £3 trillion, underscoring finance minister John Healey's challenge in his first budget next week.

item.title: Dollar holds steady as Middle East tensions simmer, oil rises
item.description: The dollar held steady against most major currencies on Wednesday as investors weighed developments in the Middle East conflict, which has revived demand for the US currency as a safe haven amid concerns about oil-driven inflation.
item.dc:creator: Shashwat Chauhan
item.content:encoded: The dollar held steady against most major currencies on Wednesday as investors weighed developments in the Middle East conflict, which has revived demand for the US currency as a safe haven amid concerns about oil-driven inflation. The euro slipped 0.1% to $1.122 and is now down almost 1% this month. Traders remained cautious on the single currency as France grapples with widespread anti-government protests and a worsening fiscal outlook that has pushed its 10-year borrowing costs to 24-year highs. "The French debt situation isn't tractable. They do need to go in and make proper adjustments on the fiscal side to get this debt level down to at least show the seriousness around the trajectory," said John Hardy, global head of macro strategy at Saxo in Copenhagen. "It's a concern (for the euro), but it's not a panic by any means just yet." France will [USN:L6N4660DJ TEXT:"deploy troops alongside police"] and mount a major security operation ahead of further protests planned for Saturday, the government said on Tuesday, acknowledging shortcomings in its response to violence last weekend. Sterling inched 0.1% up to $1.338. Data showed UK inflation rose more than expected last month, [USN:L8N46708O TEXT:"strengthening the case "]for a Bank of England rate increase in November and adding pressure on the government to support households in next week's budget. The pound rose 0.1% against the euro, up for the fifth straight session and at its strongest level in 17 months, pinning the European common currency down at 83.86 pence. The yen firmed at 157.96 per dollar. Bank of Japan Deputy Governor [USN:L1N46703F TEXT:"Ryozo Himino"] said underlying inflation was close to the central bank's 2% target and financial conditions remained loose, signalling scope for higher borrowing costs. The dollar index , which measures the US currency against six peers, was little changed at 101.7 after declining almost 0.3% on Tuesday and touching 101.50, its lowest since October 1. Investors have gravitated towards the dollar this week as volatility has increased amid the US-Israeli war with Iran, with the currency also benefiting from the relative insulation provided by US energy independence. Oil prices [USN:L1N46701N TEXT:"gained"] more than $2 a barrel on Wednesday after [USN:P8N3Z005D TEXT:"Iran said"] there was little reason to expect diplomatic progress with the US. Iran had told Pakistan's army chief there would be no talks with Washington until its demands were met, Iranian media outlet Nournews reported on Tuesday, adding that a Qatari delegation had arrived in Tehran. There was no official confirmation of the reports. Despite its safe-haven appeal, the dollar has come under pressure this month from falling Treasury yields as investors sought the relative safety of government bonds amid volatility in AI-related stocks ahead of major technology earnings. That reporting season got under way overnight with[USN:L4N4661M0 TEXT:" results from SpaceX"] (SPCX.O) . "With equity market sentiment and the growth outlook closely tied to the performance of the major tech firms, their earnings results can have a large bearing on the USD," said Carol Kong, economist and currency strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia, in a client note. The Australian dollar climbed to a three-week high and was last up 0.4% at $0.703. Reserve Bank of Australia Deputy Governor Andrew Hauser told [USN:L1N4660RH TEXT:"a Citi conference"] that the inflation outlook looked "materially worse". The New Zealand dollar inched 0.1% up to $0.569, while the Canadian dollar was broadly steady at C$1.404. Norway's crown extended gains to a seventh session, up 0.4% against the dollar. Elsewhere, the Indonesian rupiah inched 0.1% lower after the country's central bank left its [USN:L4N466083 TEXT:"main interest rate"] unchanged for a fourth straight policy review, but hiked the deposit facility rate.

item.title: Oil prices jump $2 as Iran knocks hopes of diplomatic progress
item.description: Oil prices jumped by more than $2 on Wednesday after Iran said there was little reason to expect diplomatic progress with the US, leaving the Brent benchmark hovering near five-month highs, with further market support from falling US crude and product inventories.
item.dc:creator: Shadia Nasralla
item.content:encoded: Oil prices jumped by more than $2 on Wednesday after Iran said there was [USN:P8N3Z005D TEXT:"little reason"] to expect diplomatic progress with the US, leaving the Brent benchmark hovering near five-month highs, with further market support from falling US crude and product inventories. Brent crude futures gained $2.06, or 1.9%, to $110.85 a barrel by 1048 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude was up $2.13, or 2.2%, at $99.95. In the previous session, Brent hit its highest in five months while WTI touched a six-month peak before prices fell back on discussions on [USN:S8N455017 TEXT:"mediation efforts"] in a meeting between Iran's president and Pakistan's army chief in Tehran. On Wednesday, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told the Financial Times that Iran was fully prepared to defend itself and President Masoud Pezeshkian [USN:S8N43Z00N TEXT:"told state media"] the US could not expect dialogue while blockading and threatening Iran. "Neither of the two geopolitical conflicts underpinning the market's bullish sentiment has shown any signs of de-escalation," PVM analysts said, referring to the Middle East and Russia-Ukraine wars. At least [USN:L1N46601X TEXT:"18 vessel attacks"] were recorded over the past two weeks, Kpler data showed, while LSEG analysts warned that Iran was targeting tankers well beyond the Strait of Hormuz, reaching into the Gulf of Oman and jeopardising Gulf crude loadings and ship-to-ship transfers supporting regional loadings. Iran-aligned Houthis on Monday claimed responsibility for [USN:S8N44M08Y TEXT:"attacks"] on a Saudi Aramco site in Yanbu, the Shaybah oilfield and Saudi Arabia's Riyadh and Abha airports. In the US, two Energy Department officials said on Tuesday that they were working with refiners around the world to [USN:L1N4660LI TEXT:"boost fuel output."] US crude stocks [USN:L6N4661CT TEXT:"fell"] by 4.9 million barrels in the week ended October 16, with gasoline and distillate inventories also down, said market sources citing API data. Government inventories data is due at 1430 GMT.

item.title: China uses crude stockpiles, but rising oil imports may curtail draws
item.description: China tapped its massive crude oil stockpiles for the fourth month in the past five in September as rising refinery processing rates outweighed a slight recovery in oil imports.
item.dc:creator: Clyde Russell
item.content:encoded: China [USN:L4N46008R TEXT:"tapped its massive crude oil stockpiles"] for the fourth month in the past five in September as rising refinery processing rates outweighed a slight recovery in oil imports. However, the recent pattern of drawing on inventories may end in October, with crude imports poised to recover to the most since March, the last month largely unaffected by the US and Israeli war against Iran, which started on the last day of February. Refineries processed about 530,000 barrels per day (bpd) more than what was available to them from crude imports and domestic oil production, according to calculations based on official data released this week. China does not disclose the volumes of crude flowing into or out of its strategic and commercial stockpiles, but an estimate can be made by deducting the amount of oil processed from the total crude available from imports and domestic output. On this basis, imports of 9.03 million bpd and domestic production of 4.43 million bpd meant refiners had a total of 13.46 million bpd available. Refineries [USN:L4N46508D TEXT:"processed"] 13.99 million bpd, up slightly from August's 13.91 million bpd and the most since March, meaning throughput was 530,000 bpd more than available crude. The September draw on inventories was down from the 640,000 bpd in August, largely reflecting the increase in crude imports from 8.93 million bpd to September's 9.03 million, an increase of 100,000 bpd. Even though China has dipped into stockpiles in recent months, strong builds before the start of the Iran conflict mean that there is still a small surplus of crude for the first three quarters of 2026. Refiners processed 13.73 million bpd in the first nine months of the year, while imports and domestic output totalled 13.97 million bpd, leaving a surplus of 240,000 bpd. This means that despite the dramatic cut in crude imports seen since the start of the Middle East conflict, China hasn't reduced its oil stockpile, which is estimated by analysts to contain at least 1.2 billion barrels. PRICE IMPACT What the world's largest crude importer has done is cut the volume of arrivals in the face of the surge in prices as a result of the war. Global benchmark Brent futures reached a four-year high of $126.41 a barrel on April 30, up significantly from the close of $72.48 the day before the war started as the conflict shut off flows through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway through which about 20% of global crude and refined fuels moved. However, flows through the still-contested waterway have risen in recent weeks as Gulf exporters such as Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates risk attacks from Iran. This has resulted in Brent dropping to below $80 a barrel in early August, the time when Chinese refiners would have been arranging October-delivery cargoes. Increased availability and moderating prices will result in China's crude imports rising to more than 10 million bpd in October, which would be the most since the 11.79 million recorded in March. China's seaborne imports are estimated by commodity analysts Kpler at 9.02 million bpd for October, a figure that may be revised higher by as more cargoes are assessed by the end of month. In addition to the seaborne arrivals, China receives about 1 million bpd of pipeline imports from Russia and Central Asia. The likely increase in October crude imports may be enough to cover refinery processing, even if run rates recover to more usual volumes around 14.5 million bpd. The rising crude imports are already being reflected in storage data collated by EA Crude Oil Inventories. China's onshore crude inventories rose for a second week in the seven days to October 19, reaching 1.192 billion barrels, up from the 1.189 billion the prior week, the data showed. Onshore stockpiles had reached a record 1.354 billion barrels on May 4, according to the EA data, meaning they have dropped by 162 million barrels since then. However, it's worth noting that they are only down 13 million barrels from the 1.205 billion EA reported for the week ending October 20 last year. This confirms that while China has tapped inventories in recent months, it has barely touched them in annual terms, meaning the country still retains the ability to adjust crude import volumes according to prevailing prices. item.title: Tata's owners deserve to prevail in power struggle
item.description: A clash between the salt-to-steel giant's major shareholder and chair has ramifications beyond the $260 bln group. If the owners triumph, Tata will need a new leader and strategic rethink. But a victory for Chair N. Chandrasekaran would set back shareholder rights across India.
item.dc:creator: Una Galani
item.content:encoded: The chair of Tata Sons spent part of his most recent annual letter to stakeholders reflecting on the importance of building long-term institutions in India. Now N. Chandrasekaran, or Chandra as he is widely known, is locked in a power struggle that will test one of the country's most important institutions: the rights of shareholders to control a private company. The outcome has ramifications far beyond the 158-year-old conglomerate. The crisis has its roots in a botched succession process at the business empire with sprawling interests from IT services and steel to cars, and annual revenue equivalent to 4% of Indian GDP. For decades Ratan Tata served as the group's patriarch and ultimate arbiter. After his death in 2024, his half-brother Noel Tata was appointed to the role as chair of Tata Trusts, the group of charities which owns 66% of Tata Sons, with Chandra continuing to serve as the holding company's chair, a position he has held since 2017. Though Noel inherited Ratan's title, he did not retain the same power. After Tata Sons last month reappointed Chandra as chair, Noel publicly slammed the move as "illegal". The dispute leaves a group which has over a million employees and 26 listed group companies with a combined market capitalisation of $260 billion at a crossroads. The feud hinges on a disagreement over Tata’s future. Chandra and his allies favour complying with a Reserve Bank of India determination that could require Tata Sons to list its shares on the stock market. Noel and the Tata Trusts disagree, arguing that there are ways to avoid a listing. They argue that an initial public offering would weaken the group's ability to provide patient capital to strategic industries, rescue group companies in distress, and maintain the dividend stream that funds the charities' philanthropic work. Complicating matters further, actions taken by the Charity Commissioner in Tata’s home state of Maharashtra following a complaint from one of Chandra's supporters who is a trustee and director of Tata Sons has delayed the holding company's annual general meeting. That matters because the shareholders would likely oust the chair if given the opportunity to vote. Tata is vulnerable to a challenge from an emboldened board of directors because it is not a conventional family business. Its majority owner is a group of charitable trusts. So while Noel chairs the trusts he does not own the shares. Even so, the Tata Trusts have quorum rights and veto powers embedded into Tata Sons’ Articles of Association. As Mumbai-based corporate governance research firm IiAS points out , “the board has violated the basic governance principle of shareholder supremacy”. The twin regulatory disputes have fuelled speculation in Indian financial circles about outside influence. Some observers see the unusual public silence from the government in New Delhi as evidence of creeping official involvement in one of India's most important business groups. Others point the finger at [USN:L6N45G069 TEXT:"minority investors"] in Tata Sons or rival factions in corporate India. Whatever the explanation, though, the power struggle has two possible outcomes. The first is that Noel and the Tata Trusts emerge victorious. This would come at a considerable cost for the group. Chandra's exit would not only leave Tata Sons searching for a new chair but also force a leadership reshuffle affecting 14 of its group companies. The biggest risk may be at Tata Consultancy Services (TCS.NS) . Chandra joined the information technology outsourcer in 1987 and served as its CEO for eight years before moving up to the holding company. As the $94 billion giant grapples with slowing revenue from AI disruption, Chandra has become more involved in setting its strategy. His hands-on approach is understandable: the IT company generates most of its parent's dividend income and is one of India’s important contributors of foreign exchange through the services it provides to major multinationals. The leadership dispute comes as Tata is making some of the largest capital commitments in its history. It has pledged to pour investment into semiconductors, the energy transition and defence manufacturing, as well as turnaround loss-making Air India, all of which New Delhi considers strategically important. According to one person close to Chandra, he agreed to stay on as chair despite Noel’s opposition to avoid leaving the group in limbo, with action by the Charity Commissioner also preventing Tata Sons from forming a search committee for a successor. There's some logic there. Tata Sons and its partners have committed over $27 billion of capital to five new industrial ventures since 2017, according to another person familiar with the group's finances, an amount similar to total dividends and buyback proceeds received over the past decade. The second possible outcome is that Chandra prevails over the wishes of the company's controlling shareholder. That would raise far-reaching questions about the rights of owners across Indian business. If Tata Trusts cannot pick who leads Tata Sons, other business owners will fret about their authority too. Some might then think twice about handing day-to-day control to professional managers, potentially recreating the same succession planning problems now afflicting Tata. That’s significant because the country is undergoing a vast intergenerational transfer of wealth; some $1.5 trillion is expected by Hurun Research Institute to change hands over the next decade. Chandra's position looks untenable without the support of the company's majority shareholders. And while he would be difficult to replace, he is replaceable. Other possible leaders include Indian executives with global experience like Piyush Gupta, the former CEO of DBS (DBSM.SI) , Singapore’s largest bank and now non-executive India chair at sovereign investor Temasek. Splitting the roles of chair and CEO at Tata Sons could also allow for the elevation of a veteran insider like T. V. Narendran, the CEO of Tata Steel (TISC.NS) . Tata’s subsidiaries each have their own boards of directors and can withstand a few months of uncertainty about who is in charge. Beyond that, the leadership feud will start to impact decisions about hiring and capital allocation. The issue will be tested whenever shareholders eventually get to vote on Chandra’s reappointment. Several group companies own shares in Tata Sons, including Tata Steel, Tata Motors Passenger Vehicles (TAMO.NS) , Tata Chemicals (TTCH.NS) , Tata Power (TTPW.NS) and Indian Hotels (IHTL.NS) . Those units' executives will be under pressure to take sides. The battle will also test the unity of the Tata Trusts. Their boards include not only Noel and his son, Neville, but also trustees who have supported Chandra. In time, more Tata Trusts board members may switch sides. Chandra wrote in his annual letter that Tata is "building for the India of 2047" so that, when the country looks back after 100 years of independence from British rule, it finds "that the foundations were laid well". It is vital for the company and for India that Tata's owners should decide who lays them. Follow Una Galani on LinkedIn and X .

item.title: SpaceX is stuck in a difficult adolescence
item.description: The $2 trln company’s server-rental unit grew 800%, but attractive returns will probably fade as chip shortages subside. Rockets are boss Elon Musk’s durable advantage, but mostly as a way to support the next big thing. AI, wireless networks, chipmaking or even cars beckon.
item.dc:creator: Robert Cyran
item.content:encoded: What will SpaceX (SPCX.O) be when it grows up? The limitless possibility of a long-prolonged corporate adolescence supported the rocket, satellite network and artificial intelligence company’s ascent to a $2 trillion valuation. Results released on Tuesday highlight the quick returns boss Elon Musk has gleaned from opportunistically expanding into new areas like renting out chips for chatbots. Yet that business could soon erode, leaving the impulsive CEO to search out yet another focus from the many available. SpaceX said that its AI and server-rental unit – renamed to “Super Intelligence,” following President Donald Trump’s preferred terminology – generated an astonishing $7.6 billion of revenue in the third quarter, an 829% increase from last year. This surprise success was the product of arrested development: Musk wanted to run a top AI lab, yet his Grok bot’s also-ran status left its data centers underused. More-popular rivals like Anthropic conversely face a shortage, and paid top dollar to get chips now. This happy accident is now SpaceX’s biggest business line, overtaking its original core focus of putting satellites into orbit with reusable rockets. Chief Financial Officer Bret Johnsen boasted in September that incremental investment in Super Intelligence pays back [USN:L6N45T0Y8 TEXT:"rapidly"], and so the company has said that it could increase capacity perhaps five-fold by the end of next year. High returns, however, stem from chip shortages, which have lifted rental prices above where they were last year. Markets seem to expect this situation to wane: the price to rent out Nvidia GB300 silicon is about $10 an hour for the next several months, analysts at MoffettNathanson estimated, but only $4 further in the future. If AI demand is lower than expected, or chief clients like Anthropic are stretched too thin, prices could plummet lower. If becoming a cloud operator is just an adolescent phase for SpaceX, then what’s next? There’s always enterprise software, like the promised “Macrohard,” an AI platform to augment workers. The company’s satellite broadband business threatens to take on [USN:L6N4511C3 TEXT:"wireless networks"] worldwide. And SpaceX is building a $17 billion, 100-million-square foot plant for fabricating semiconductors with partner Tesla (TSLA.O) . If Musk chose to [USN:L6N42B10Y TEXT:"jam together"] the two companies fully, cars and robots are added to the menu. Rockets, ironically, fade into obscurity. Revenue for SpaceX’s namesake business grew only 6% compared to last year. It is simply too small to justify such a wild valuation, which was 94 times estimated earnings over the next year before quarterly figures were released. Yet the company [USN:L6N41315K TEXT:"dominates the market"] for putting stuff into orbit, while electric vehicles are beset by rising Chinese rivals, some 200 companies build AI data centers for hire, and countless robot developers pop up. Endless opportunity beckons, just not in the places where SpaceX is actually mature. Follow Robert Cyran on Bluesky . SpaceX said on October 20 that it generated $14.6 billion of revenue in the third quarter, compared to $5.6 billion in the same period a year prior. The company’s Super Intelligence segment produced revenue of $7.6 billion, up from $813 million a year ago. The company earned $4.4 billion of net income, as opposed to a $1.1 billion loss a year ago. Capital expenditures nearly tripled to $19.6 billion, as the company invested $16.4 billion in Super Intelligence. CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: Nvidia emerges as the central bank of AI
item.description: The $5.3 trln firm has helped prop up buyers of its own chips, including under-pressure data-center operator CoreWeave. Boss Jensen Huang says that the so-called neocloud is strong enough to stand on its own. A freeze in credit markets could force his hand.
item.dc:creator: Pranav Kiran
item.content:encoded: Call it the Bank of Jensen. Chipmaker Nvidia’s (NVDA.O) outspoken CEO Jensen Huang has pledged massive support to keep the artificial intelligence economy humming. That includes a backstop for CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , whose shares are slumping as it burns cash to stuff data centers with Nvidia chips. Huang insists that the so-called neocloud is strong enough to stand alone. If lenders grow leery, though, the $5.3 trillion chipmaker’s role as a kind of central bank for the industry could be tested. Neoclouds borrow money to build server farms for blue-chip tech giants like Microsoft (MSFT.O) through to AI labs like Anthropic. Long-term contracts fetch about $10 million per megawatt of capacity and can give lenders confidence to fork over billions in debt. Yet truly juicy pricing, of perhaps $40 million per megawatt, goes to shorter-term deals. With interest rates rising and neocloud debt selling off, the risk is that cheaper deals no longer clear companies’ cost of capital while funding becomes too stringent to chase richer opportunities. Huang, like any good central banker, has been trying to ensure liquidity. Nvidia not only invested [USN:L4N3YR124 TEXT:"$2 billion"] in CoreWeave’s equity, but in September inked a $6.3 billion agreement to purchase any unsold capacity through 2032. That should help smooth a move away from long-term contracts. The company employs credit facilities that pair chip purchases with specific customer contracts against which they’re secured. Early versions matched the maturity of the facility with the length of the contract. A more recent iteration, however, raised five-year debt against three-year agreements, introducing renewal risk. Nvidia should be able to help defray that by being a customer of last resort. It’s important for Huang to keep this market humming: customers including neoclouds accounted for 45% of Nvidia’s $89 billion in data-center revenue last quarter, with so-called hyperscalers like Microsoft making up the rest, according to Visible Alpha data. Bank of America analysts [USN:L6N44N16H TEXT:"reckon"] that Nvidia’s backstop commitments across the AI ecosystem total $230 billion. The real nightmare scenario is that neoclouds can’t renew contracts, or that customers begin to default, destabilizing the guarantees on which lenders depend and freezing them out of credit markets. This is, to be clear, hypothetical. But it would threaten a massive source of demand for Nvidia. At that point, Huang’s backstops would be tested. The Federal Reserve was able to extend vast support to the economy when credit froze up during the 2008 crisis. But Nvidia is not actually a money-printing central bank: presumably, if its customers suffer, so too will its own cash flow. The company can only sustain the AI boom so far. Follow Pranav Kiran on Bluesky and X . “CoreWeave’s strength is improving every day,” Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told Bloomberg at an event on October 15 in Stockholm. “I’m optimistic. Their cost of capital is actually decreasing.” CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: Netflix morphs into same couch potato it smashed
item.description: A leadership shakeup and job cuts follow an estimated 25% drop in new monthly subscribers, to 1.2 mln, over the past year. Its botched Warner Bros deal also accentuated struggles that evoke ones the streamer inflicted on cable TV. Absent creative sparks, a similar fate awaits.
item.dc:creator: Jennifer Saba
item.content:encoded: Netflix (NFLX.O) is in danger of starring in a financial version of "Squid Game." Slowdowns in subscriber and revenue growth, along with its botched $83 billion deal to buy Warner Bros., threaten to leave the pioneering streaming service fighting for its life like the contestants in its most popular show ever. The company's top line for the three months ending in September is projected to rise nearly 12% from a year earlier, according to estimates gathered by LSEG. It would be the slowest rate in 11 quarters. Co-Chief Executive Ted Sarandos bluntly said last month that he was not happy with the trajectory. Netflix trimmed 6% of its [USN:L6N4600X7 TEXT:"workforce,"] or about 1,000 people, and is shaking up leadership. Peter Rice, a former Walt Disney and Fox executive, will be overseeing both content and film, replacing two ousted executives who previously held the roles. There has not been enough hit programming, like its adaptation of John Steinbeck's “East of Eden” featuring Florence Pugh. As a result, Netflix clocked 1.2 million new subscribers in September, 25% fewer than during the same month in 2025, according to data cruncher Antenna. Such deceleration probably helps explain the desire to acquire rival HBO and the Warner Bros studio, which ultimately were sold to Paramount instead. The splashy acquisition proposal nevertheless rattled shareholders accustomed to a company that builds rather than buys, and put a brighter spotlight on Netflix's struggles. Under founder Reed Hastings, Netflix upended the cushy world of cable and satellite TV, and their monthly bundles, by going to consumers directly with an independent offering available over the internet. The new model forced incumbents to consolidate as their technology-focused competitor spent heavily and commanded a valuation of some 300 times earnings. It now trades at about 19 times the projected bottom line over the next 12 months. The multiple is a healthy premium to Comcast's six times, and even Walt Disney's 15 times. Even so, Netflix now finds itself seeking ways to avoid becoming one of the same couch potatoes it smashed, as YouTube, TikTok and other apps attract younger and bigger audiences. Finding and producing programming that appeals to wide audiences is always hit or miss in Hollywood, and new ideas and formats inevitably come around. As the dystopian "Squid Game" made all too clear, capitalism is merciless. Follow Jennifer Saba on Bluesky and LinkedIn . Netflix is due to report its quarterly financial results on October 20, with revenue expected to grow 12% from a year earlier, according to estimates compiled by LSEG. The streaming service cut 6% of its workforce, or 1,000 employees, its biggest reduction since 2022, Reuters reported on October 14, citing an internal memo. CONTEXT-NEWS

item.title: Iran tells Pakistan army chief no talks with Washington until demands are met
item.description: Pakistan is a key intermediary between the United States and Iran.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Iran told Pakistan's army chief on Tuesday that there would be no talks with Washington until Tehran's demands were met, Iranian media reported, underscoring its hardening stance despite mediation efforts by key interlocutor Pakistan. President Masoud Pezeshkian discussed mediation efforts and regional developments with Field Marshal Asim Munir in Tehran, according to Nournews. Pakistan is a key intermediary between the United States and Iran. Earlier mediation efforts helped produce an [USN:L1N42P0Q6 TEXT:"interim peace agreement"] in June, but the Islamabad Memorandum quickly unravelled as fighting between Iran and the US resumed weeks after. Munir also met Iranian parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who said Washington could not regain Tehran's trust until it fulfilled [USN:S8N43Z003 TEXT:"seven conditions"] Iran set last month for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, according to an Iranian readout of the meeting. The demands include ending a US blockade on its ports, the lifting of sanctions on its oil exports as well as ending hostilities on all regional fronts. Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, delivered a similar message during a separate meeting with Munir, saying there would be [USN:L8N46515R TEXT:"no talks"] with Washington until Tehran's demands were met, according to Iranian media. Rezaei also said all enriched nuclear materials would remain in Iran, reiterating Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei's [USN:L8N41X1O4 TEXT:"position"] that near-weapons-grade uranium should not be shipped abroad. US Vice President JD Vance said [USN:L6N45S099 TEXT:"earlier this month"] that Iran must make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity to satisfy US demands and end the countries' eight-month-old war. Israel, the United States and other Western states have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, including pointing to its move to enrich uranium to 60%, far higher than needed for civilian uses and closer to the 90% needed for a weapon. Iran denies seeking nuclear weapons.

item.title: Microsoft pulls out of UK Nscale data centre deal over power delay
item.description: Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor a flagship data centre for Nvidia-backed Nscale after power connection delays pushed its expected supply date into the 2030s, highlighting a major obstacle to Britain's AI ambitions.
item.dc:creator: Paul Sandle
item.content:encoded: Microsoft (MSFT.O) has pulled out of a deal to anchor a flagship data centre for Nvidia-backed (NVDA.O) Nscale after power connection delays pushed its expected supply date into the 2030s, highlighting a major obstacle to Britain's AI ambitions. The US tech giant said on Monday it remained committed to its partnership with Nscale, including work to build digital infrastructure and support AI growth globally. "This decision relates to a single site," a Microsoft spokesperson said of its termination of an agreement for the data centre in Loughton, Essex, where Nscale had faced delays, with electricity grid officials telling the AI company they did not expect to supply power to the site until the 2030s. "Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," a spokesperson for Nscale told Reuters. "We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK, and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, as well as other expansion sites in the UK," they added. Microsoft's move was first reported by the Telegraph newspaper. The project was among [USN:L5N3V30O9 TEXT:"technology"] deals announced during US President Donald Trump's visit in September 2025 and intended to showcase Britain's ambition to become a global AI leader. But that faces a major constraint in the form of electricity supply, with bottlenecks in grid connection queues delaying data centre projects by as long as 13 years. The Loughton site was due to begin operating early next year, with 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs providing 50 megawatts of AI computing capacity to help power Microsoft's Azure services in Britain, the companies said last year. Nscale filed for an initial public offering in the United States last month, with Microsoft and Anthropic expected to be among its major customers, according to its prospectus. The group provides infrastructure, including computing capacity, power and data centres, as well as software for training and running AI models. Nscale has grown rapidly since launch, increasing its total contracted value from $100 million to more than $103 billion in two-and-a-half years. It competes with AI infrastructure providers CoreWeave (CRWV.O) , Nebius (NBIS.O) , Crusoe and Lambda.
